items: On the fifth evening the singer came slowly, as a man comes to heavy work.
The oath is awake, you said. Sing what it woke, father.

It woke everything, child: every harbor, every forge, every mother's fear in Greece. Tonight I sing the mustering — and I warn you now, the war does not begin well. It begins by striking the wrong country.
Muse, sing through me the gathering of the kings: the summons of the oath, the madman's plow, the sign of the serpent — and the nine long years written in it.
Hear then, as the Muse gives it.
When the word of Menelaus reached Mycenae, Agamemnon did not weep for his brother. He began to count.
Every king who stood at the horse-sacrifice swore to defend this marriage against any man on earth. Very well. Send to every king who swore.

And the heralds went out to every royal hall in Greece, carrying two words: THE OATH. Some kings rose gladly, smelling plunder. Some rose grimly, keeping faith. Some looked for a way out. All rose. An oath sworn on blood does not offer a third choice.

And Agamemnon, counting the kings who must now follow his house to war, understood what his brother's loss had bought him: the high command of all Greece. Grief is grief, princes. But watch what men build with it.
In sandy Pylos the summons came to Nestor — oldest of the kings, who had ruled three generations of men. He did not hesitate the length of one breath.
Gather them at Aulis, sons of Atreus — the one bay that can hold a thousand keels. And fetch the clever ones first: an army is spears, but a war is minds. Fetch me the Ithacan.

Look well at this old man, princes of Miletus. Nestor of Pylos — from whose house, through Neleus his father, your own line is sprung. When I sing him, I sing your grandfathers' grandfather. He alone of all these kings will come home from this war with clean hands and a whole heart. Ask yourselves, as we go, how he manages it.

But on Ithaca the heralds found a ruin. Odysseus — the mind that had tied the oath — met them plowing the beach with an ox and an ass yoked as a team, sowing the furrows with salt, singing to himself. A madman cannot swear. A madman cannot sail.
With the heralds had come Palamedes of Nauplia — a lord almost as famous for cleverness as Odysseus himself. And cleverness knows cleverness, princes, the way one forger knows another's coin.
A beautiful son, lady. Let him greet his father.
And he laid the child in the furrow, in the path of the team.
The plow turned. Of course it turned. No man alive could have held that furrow — and so the whole beach knew that the plowman was a man alive, and sane, and caught.

Three words, and courteous ones. But mark that look, princes, and enter it in the ledger. Odysseus forgave many things in his long life. Being beaten at his own art was never one of them. Palamedes has perhaps eight years to live.

So the kings kept the oath, and Greece emptied into one bay. From rocky Ithaca and sandy Pylos, from Crete of the hundred cities, from Salamis and Argos and Tiryns of the great walls — more ships than the sea had ever carried, under one command: Agamemnon, lord of Mycenae, king of kings.

The full count of the ships I will sing in its own place, as the great singer does, when they stand off Troy at last. Tonight, only know: the world had never seen the like. And it was about to sail the wrong way.
At the altars by the spring, under the one great plane tree, the kings made offering for the sailing. And the gods answered — but not from the fire.
A serpent, back blood-red, ran from beneath the altar and up the tree — to a sparrow's nest on the highest bough: eight nestlings, and the mother that hatched them made nine.
It devoured all nine. And the god who sent it turned it to stone where it coiled, in the sight of the whole army. Silence, princes, is the loudest sound ten thousand men can make.

Hear it, Achaeans! Nine the serpent swallowed — nine years shall you war and win nothing. But in the TENTH year the wide-wayed city falls. Zeus of the counsels has shown it: late-fulfilled, but its fame shall never die!
Ten years. Watch each king hear it, and you know each king.

Remember this sign with me, old king. There will come a day, deep in those nine years, when this whole army will break for the ships and home — and one of us will have to stand in their way and remind them what the god promised. Remember it with me.
Enter it in the ledger, princes: a promise of Zeus, and a man saving it for the hour of despair. You will see him spend it.
So they sailed — a thousand ships, ten thousand spears, and not one man aboard who knew the way to Troy.

Understand it, princes: the sea-roads east were traders' secrets, and no trader sat on that flagship. They knew Troy lay east, and that Asia was wide. It was enough for pride. It is never enough for war.
And when a rich coast rose against the evening — walls, herds, a river — Agamemnon looked at it and saw what he had come to see. "Troy," said the king of kings. It was not Troy.

They fell on Teuthrania of the Mysians as on Troy — beach and granary and town. The Mysians had stolen no queen and sworn no oath. They fought because armed strangers were burning their homes. There is a lesson here so plain I will not insult you by speaking it.

And here, princes — in the wrong war, on the wrong beach — the song first shows you its greatest name. Achilles, son of Peleus and the sea-goddess Thetis: sixteen years old, faster than the rest of mankind, and already worth half the army. Beside him, as always, from now until the hour that breaks the world: Patroclus.

But Mysia had a king worth an army too: Telephus — a son of Heracles himself. Yes, princes: the blood of the hero of the first song, standing against the Greeks. The old threads never leave this loom.
Telephus killed Thersander of Thebes, a king in his own right, and rolled the whole landing back toward the sea. The blood of Heracles was paying for its ground.

Then the earth itself betrayed him: a vine — a vine, on a war-beach — took his ankle like a snare. The vine belongs to Dionysus, whose rites Telephus had once slighted. No debt sleeps forever, princes; some merely wait for the worst possible moment. That is rather their point.

And Achilles was on him, and the ash spear of Pelion — Chiron's wedding-gift, that only he could lift — drank its first blood: the thigh of a son of Heracles. Mark the wound. The whole war will hang from it before we are done tonight.
Then a grey prisoner was dragged before the kings, and he was not crying for mercy. He was crying a name. "MYSIA," he cried. "This is MYSIA, madmen. Troy is NORTH."

So the first blood of the great war for the oath of Tyndareus was Mysian blood, owed by no one, shed for nothing. The kings stood among the burning boats of strangers and understood what they had done. Some wars begin with a crime, princes. This one managed to begin with a blunder AND a crime, and had not yet seen Troy.
They re-embarked in shame — and the sky, which had watched it all, decided it had seen enough.
The storm took the thousand ships and dealt them like a thrown deck across the whole Aegean. The first mustering of the Greeks ended with no two kings in sight of one another.
They limped home singly, king by king, over weeks — to wives who asked how the war had gone, a question with no bearable answer.
And one storm-thread the gods wove with particular care: the ship of Achilles they drove to the island of Scyros. Nothing in this song is only weather, princes.
King Lycomedes of Scyros took the shipwrecked heroes in, as guest-law commands. He had a daughter, Deidamia.

The ships needed a season's mending, and the season was kind. Before it ended, Achilles and Deidamia were wed. It was — hear this and keep it, princes — the one purely happy thing that ever happened to that shining and doomed young man. One island season. The gods do not give him another.

And when the summons found him and he sailed, Deidamia carried his child. Enter the ledger's largest entry, princes: the son of Achilles — Neoptolemus, "new-war." He will be born after his father sails, grow up on this island, and come to Troy only when... no. That is the end of the song, and this is its beginning. But remember Scyros.

*Some later singers tell of Achilles hidden on Scyros among the king's daughters in a girl's dress, found out by a trick of Odysseus. The old song of the Cycle knows only the storm and the marriage, and I sing the old song.
Father — the Mysian dead. Who pays for THEM? They were no part of the oath, the theft, the plan. Does heaven's ledger have a page for the wrong country?

...That, child, is the best question anyone has asked me in this hall, and I will not cheapen it with a neat answer. The songs are silent on the Mysian dead. Perhaps the silence is the answer. Perhaps the silence is the wound. When you are a king, remember that the songs go silent exactly where kings most need them to speak.
But one Mysian the song does follow — because his wound would not heal.
The spear-wound of Achilles festered in Telephus year after year, past every herb and every prayer — for it was no common spear, and heaven does not let its instruments heal at random.
Until the god at last gave him a riddle for his pain: THE WOUNDER SHALL HEAL. Nothing else. Gods bill by the word, princes, and every word costs a journey.

So the son of Heracles wrapped himself in a beggar's cloak and sailed — alone, in pain, into the country of his enemies — to ask the man who ruined him to mend him. Weigh the courage of that, princes, against all the shield-glory in this song. I know where I set my own weight.

He came to Mycenae as a beggar, and when the guards would have taken him, he did the one thing no Greek hand could answer: he took up the king's own infant son, Orestes, and knelt with him upon the holy hearth — suppliant of the hearth, holding the house's heir. Now every law of heaven stood armed around him.

Look long at this picture, princes; the loom is showing its threads. The baby in the suppliant's arms will one day avenge this house. The woman in the doorway, watching her husband's raised hand, is learning tonight how that hand weighs a child's life against a king's need. She will have cause to remember. And the ragged man on the hearth is the son of Heracles, teaching the whole heroic world its own deepest law: that the helpless suppliant is stronger than the armed king. File it all away. The song forgets nothing.
I am no physician. I never learned the healing herbs — Chiron taught me spears, not simples. How can I heal what I cannot even name?
Because the oracle never named YOU, son of Peleus. "The wounder shall heal." What wounded him? Not the man. The SPEAR. Bring the ash of Pelion — and a scraping-blade.

They scraped the rust of the great spear into the wound — and the wound that no herb could touch began to close before their eyes. The wounder healed. Write the rule on your hearts, princes, for this song will use it again and again until the very end: WHAT HARMS IS WHAT CURES, and the road back always runs through the thing itself. Remember the spear-rust when you meet a wooden horse.
You have your healing, Mysian. Now the fee: the sea-road to Troy. You know it. Sail with us and pilot the fleet.

I will guide you to Troy's shore — that, for my healing. But I will not draw spear against the city. Priam's own sister is my wife, Greeks; my son Eurypylus is half of Troy's blood. A man does not war on his wife's kin. Guide, yes. Fight, never.

And that was honorably said, and honorably kept. But enter the son in the ledger, princes: Eurypylus, half Heracles and half Troy. Years from now, when Troy is desperate and Achilles is dust, that boy — grown terrible — will be bought to Troy's wall by a gift of a golden vine, and the son of Achilles will meet him there. The spear that healed the father will not spare the son. The loom is patient.

Then the years passed — for a muster broken must be gathered again, and kingdoms bled by a false war must refill. The songs count differently; count with me simply: years, while the oath lay banked like a covered fire.

On Ithaca, Telemachus learned to run on the beach where his father had plowed salt. Odysseus watched his son grow and his olive-tree bed stand rooted, and knew to the day how much happiness he was being allowed to bank. Clever men suffer worst, princes: they see the bill coming.

And in Troy, Helen of Sparta — Helen of Troy now, as the world was learning to say — sat at her loom and wove. And what she wove, the great singer will tell you when he finds her at it years hence: the battles of Trojans and Greeks, fought for her sake. She was weaving this song, princes, before most of it had happened. Some knowledge needs no seer's fillet. Some knowledge is just a mirror.
Telephus knows the road. The ships are new-tarred, the boys are grown to spearmen. Send to every king a second time: AULIS. And this time, no man's plow and no man's madness excuses him.
And Greece rose the second time — heavier, grimmer, better. The first muster had been a festival with weapons. This one was a war.
Ajax of Salamis, a wall that walked. Diomedes of Argos, keen as a whetted edge. Idomeneus of Crete, grave and sure. The suitors of the wedding-court, princes — come to pay the wedding's bill.
And last came fifty black ships from Phthia, rowed in perfect time and perfect silence, and the whole armada stopped its noise to watch them beach. The Myrmidons had come.

Achilles came down the beach, and grown kings who had sacked cities felt their throats go dry. He was worth ships beyond counting, and every man there knew it — none better than the king of kings, who owned the command but not the flame. File THAT away too, princes. It is the seed of the greatest song of all.

And out past the surf, where no one looked, the sea stood a little taller than the sea. Thetis watched her son walk up the sand into his short forever. She knew the two fates over him — the long dim life, the brief blazing one — and she knew which one walks off a ship at Aulis.
And Troy heard. This time there was no error in the sea-roads and no doubt in the reports: the greatest fleet in the world's history was massing, and its heading was the Hellespont.

Grain into the citadel. The springs walled. Watch-fires the length of the coast. And heralds to every ally from the Axius to Lycia — Troy calls in her own oaths now. If they come, they will find no sleeping city.

And Priam watched Hector — thirty years old, and already the best man in this entire song; yes, princes, I said what I said, and I will stand behind it at the end — and the old king thought: whatever my second son has broken, my first may yet hold. Half of that thought will prove true.
The armament is whole, lord of gods. The guide is bound. The instrument of wrath — the son of Peleus — walks the beach at Aulis.
Let them sail and not stop.
The two rejected queens of heaven had waited years already. Their hatred had not cooled. Such hatred does not cool; it compounds.

But one goddess looked down at Aulis with other thoughts — the lady of the wild things, whose grove stood at the bay's edge, and whose eyes miss nothing that runs on four feet or boasts on two. Her hour is tomorrow's song. Tonight she only watches.

On the last evening, Agamemnon stood above his thousand ships, and the singer will do him justice: he had built this. The oath was Odysseus's device, the wrong was Paris's, but the ARMY was his — gathered twice, fed, held together by his will. He was, that evening, the greatest king the Greek world had ever produced.
Look at him, Ithacan. A great king at the flood of his greatness.
I am looking, old man. And I am thinking that the flood is exactly when a man should watch his footing — and that he is not thinking that at all.

Pride is not a sin in this song, princes — every hero in it is proud, and rightly. But there is a line where pride stops measuring itself against men and starts measuring itself against heaven. Watch the king of kings walk toward that line. He is one boast away.

At the edge of the bay stood an old grove, sacred to Artemis of the wild things, and in it that evening a hind moved between the oaks — white-flanked, beautiful, unafraid, as beasts are unafraid only on ground where they are under a god's hand.

And from the dune above his ships, the king of kings marked her. That is all that happened that evening, princes. A king saw a deer on a god's ground and thought a thought. Tomorrow you will hear the thought spoken aloud, and what it costs. Tonight, only mark how quietly the greatest griefs choose their doors.
The wind, for now, blew fair for Troy.

So ends the mustering: the oath honored, the error paid for in shame, the road known, the fleet whole, the wind fair. Ten thousand fires on the water, and around each one, men who believed they would be home in the tenth autumn.
Some of them will be. Fewer than believe it.
And above the altars, the stone serpent kept its count in the moonlight. Nine years, said the stone. Nine years, and the tenth. The stone, at least, would be proven exactly right.

Father... every person in tonight's song was doing his duty. The kings kept the oath. Palamedes served the muster. Telephus defended his land. Achilles fought where his king pointed. And the sum of all those duties was a burned country that owed nothing and a beach full of Mysian dead.

Yes. You have found the second riddle of the song, child — the brother of the first. Fate and freedom was the first. This is the harder one: how faithful men, each keeping his own right law, can weave together a wrong that none of them chose. The songs do not solve it. The songs only make sure you cannot look away from it.
And tomorrow it sharpens to its finest point — one man, one duty, one daughter. Sleep, if you can.
Enough. The fleet is whole at Aulis, the guide aboard, the wind fair — and a king has seen a deer in a goddess's grove.
Tomorrow the wind fails, child. Tomorrow: a boast, a becalmed sea, a seer's terrible price — and a girl who comes to Aulis dressed for a wedding. Then Troy at last. I promise you Troy at last.
"Late come the fulfillments of Zeus, and late-shown are his signs — but their fame does not perish, and their count does not fail."
— after the reading of the sign at Aulis, as the song of the wrath remembers it.
